source.title: InfoLaw: Information Scaling Laws for Large Language Models with Quality-Weighted Mixture Data and Repetition
source.authors: Feng-Ze Liu; Wei-Dong Zhou; Bin-Bin Li; Ping Guo; Zi-Jun Wang; Bing-Ni Zhang; Yi-Fan Zhang; Yifeng Yu; Xiaohuan Zhou; Tai-Feng Wang

record.file_problem: Full paper text including appendices is present. Some equations and words have minor formatting/OCR artifacts, but the relevant results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares conventional loss-compute scaling with results under repeated, quality-weighted data and reports systematic extrapolation errors. It also proposes and tests a data-aware alternative.
record.gate_note: The study measures downstream-benchmark evaluation loss (an average perplexity derived from benchmark accuracies), not held-out pretraining loss, so V1 is not counted as tested. The study does report results on larger-scale prediction, repeated-data regimes, and downstream performance. Cited findings from other papers are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares small-run power-law extrapolations with larger-run outcomes and finds systematic failures under repeated data. It also tests downstream-performance prediction and sensitivity to data and functional-form choices. Its loss is a downstream-accuracy-derived proxy, so these results do not test held-out pretraining-loss scaling.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the authors' conclusion: InfoLaw predicts benchmark-derived evaluation loss across mixtures and larger runs, with reported pooled errors of 0.15% mean and 0.96% maximum, and qualitatively generalizes across overtraining levels. These are not held-out pretraining-loss results. RefinedWeb validation uses corpus-specific fitting, and cross-overtraining prediction has no reported numerical error.
record.recipe_differences: InfoLaw models information accumulated from quality buckets, repetition and model scale, then fits loss against that constructed quantity; the conventional comparison fits loss against compute. The paper also compares alternative normalization and λ(N) fit forms.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with repetition and data mixture. The authors report that constant and power-law decay normalizations fail where log(K) works, and that a logarithmic λ(N) fit performs best among the tested forms. RefinedWeb required searching λ values at the evaluated sizes rather than fitting a λ(N) curve.

fits_no_version.finding: An in-sample power law fits loss against a learned information quantity with alpha 3.7373 and beta 0.0441.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benchmark-derived loss can be collapsed onto a power law using a fitted quality-, repetition- and model-dependent coordinate.

fits_no_version.finding: A logarithmic function best fits the auxiliary lambda-versus-model-compute relationship among the tested families.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The auxiliary repetition-decay parameter is better modeled logarithmically than by the tested exponential or power-law alternatives.

fits_no_version.finding: Benchmark-derived loss strongly correlates with the benchmark accuracies used to construct it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The chosen transformation preserves downstream performance ordering within the evaluated regime.

record.problems: The primary experiments use 27 fitting runs across 252M–1.2B models; the larger-scale and overtraining results are not accompanied by numerical uncertainty estimates. The authors note that quality buckets use a fixed heuristic and that they did not ablate the number or boundaries of tiers. Several comparisons are described qualitatively or shown in figures without numerical values. The loss measure is downstream-benchmark-derived rather than held-out pretraining loss.
record.rows_left_out: Individual points in scaling plots and training-time curves were not extracted where the text gives no individual values; aggregate textual outcomes are recorded instead. The paper’s detailed optimal-mixture tables and data-quality benchmark comparisons were omitted because they do not directly test the listed scaling-law versions.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss and its power-law dependence on parameters, tokens or compute with other resources nonbinding.
Extrapolation of held-out pretraining loss. The reported prediction errors concern a benchmark-derived loss proxy, and errors are not separated by extrapolation distance.
Empirical optimization of parameter and token allocation across compute budgets. The study adopts an existing allocation formula rather than estimating or testing its optimality.
Controlled architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count.

Other modalities, fine-tuning and transfer; held-out pretraining-loss scaling under repetition. Successful information-coordinate fits do not establish the ordinary parameter/token/compute power-law form.
Prediction from independently measured held-out pretraining loss, and independently validated quantitative predictions for each downstream task.
Changes in compute-optimal allocation, parameter-counting effects, explanations of disagreement between published exponents, and systematic schedule comparisons.

missing.what: Appendix H explicitly reports deviations for both IST and LST curves when the conventional law is fitted on the first three points. This qualifies R2's general no-repetition success claim and introduces fitting-range dependence.

record.verdict_notes: V2 and V5 verdicts use their extrapolation and repeated-regime clauses for the explicitly identified benchmark-derived loss; they should not be read as verdicts about V1's held-out pretraining loss. Missing uncertainty alone does not justify a limits_scope verdict. No-repetition success does not contradict V7. The supplied figure text lacks readable plotted coordinates, and Appendix H's broad deviation statement cannot be numerically reconciled with the main text's no-repetition success statement.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not report held-out pretraining loss; its evaluation loss is derived from downstream benchmark accuracies.
The study tests prediction of downstream-benchmark evaluation loss, not held-out pretraining loss, and does not test all model or training regimes.
It searches data-mixture recipes for fixed model/token settings but does not test how loss-minimising parameter and token counts grow with compute.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Tests repeated and overtrained text-pretraining regimes only; no other modalities, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Reports associations between validation loss and downstream benchmark performance, but does not test downstream-task prediction from held-out pretraining loss across general settings.
Tests sensitivity to data repetition, normalization and functional-fit choices, but not parameter-counting or training-schedule choices in general.

rows.subject: LayerMix-trained model runs (aggregate; fit range 252M–1.2B, extrapolated to larger models)
rows.size_stated: 252M–1.2B fitting range; larger models used for extrapolation
rows.operation_detail: Compared conventional power-law loss-compute fits with realized evaluation loss under repeated LayerMix data.

conditions.value: LayerMix with repetition; representative HQ and MLQ recipes

rows.measure: Average perplexity over five downstream tasks versus compute
rows.baseline: Conventional power-law scaling curve fitted on 252M–1.2B runs
rows.value: The conventional curve systematically mis-extrapolates under repetition, yielding overly optimistic loss reductions as compute increases.
rows.note: Aggregate result for the repeated-data runs. The paper says the failure appears consistently across representative mixture recipes.
rows.check: Accurate conventional extrapolation is absent for the benchmark-derived loss; this is positive evidence for V7's curve-deviation clause. It does not establish failure of held-out pretraining-loss scaling. The fitting range spans model sizes rather than independently varying parameters, tokens and compute.

source_check.correct: Accurate conventional extrapolation is absent under repetition; setup-dependent departures from a compute power law are observed for V7. These links require different states.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.2, Figure 1; Section 6, comparison with traditional scaling laws.
source_check.problem: The single absent state incorrectly describes the positive evidence for V7.

rows.subject: LayerMix-trained model runs (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared loss-compute behavior in a regime with negligible repetition against the repeated-data regime.

conditions.value: No repetition; large source (S ≫ K), including Random and HQ IST

rows.value: The traditional scaling law performs well on data without repetition.
rows.note: Reported as an aggregate comparison; no numerical values are stated in the text.
rows.check: The no-repetition comparison is a control for setup dependence, not evidence against V7. Remove V5 because this condition does not test the repeated-data extension. Appendix H also says IST curves deviate when fitted on the first three points, qualifying the general assertion that conventional scaling works without repetition.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3; Appendix E, Figure 5(a); Appendix H.

rows.subject: 850M HQ LST and 850M MQ LST runs
rows.operation_detail: Compared evaluation-loss trajectories over training for two LayerMix recipes with different repetition levels.

conditions.value: Top 5% bucket repeated roughly 16× for HQ and roughly 10× for MQ

rows.measure: Evaluation loss over training and final loss
rows.value: The runs have similar early-training evaluation loss; the more repetitive HQ run improves substantially more slowly later and ends with worse loss.
rows.note: The described comparison concerns training-time evaluation loss, not held-out pretraining loss.
rows.check: The late-training divergence supports dependence on repetition and mixture. Two trajectories at one model size do not independently test a power-law form, so remove V5. Quality weights and repetition change together; this is not an isolated repetition intervention.

rows.subject: LayerMix experiments used to fit InfoLaw (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Fit a power law between evaluation loss and the proposed quality-, repetition-, token-, and model-aware information quantity.

conditions.value: HQ, MQ and LQ LayerMix recipes

rows.note: This is a power law in the study's constructed information metric, not directly in parameter count, tokens, or compute.
rows.check: This is an in-sample fit against a constructed, fitted information quantity. It neither tests extrapolation nor establishes the same power-law form in parameters, tokens or compute. Retain as method description rather than independent scaling evidence.

rows.subject: LayerMix runs on unseen scales and unseen mixture weights (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated InfoLaw predictions on unseen mixture recipes and larger model scales using parameters fitted on the smaller runs.

conditions.value: MLQ, MHQ and 25 randomly sampled weight sets

rows.measure: Absolute error between predicted and measured validation loss
rows.baseline: InfoLaw prediction fitted on the 252M–1.2B data
rows.value: 0.15% average absolute error and 0.96% maximum error on all unseen data points.
rows.note: Aggregate across the stated unseen data points; the abstract also describes prediction up to a 7B model trained on 425B tokens.
rows.check: The reported errors pool recipe generalization and scale extrapolation; they are not separately reported for the largest models. Remove V5 and V7: predictive success using a constructed information coordinate does not independently establish ordinary power-law scaling or fit dependence.

rows.subject: 1.2B model runs
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated predicted and measured validation loss across 25 held-out LayerMix configurations.
rows.measure: Pearson correlation between predicted and measured validation losses
rows.note: The paper describes this as suggesting reliable ranking of recipes, but does not provide an error value for this result.
rows.check: This tests recipe ranking at fixed 1.2B size, not extrapolation to substantially larger runs or the power-law form under repetition. Pearson correlation 0.76 measures imperfect association, not calibrated prediction error.

source_check.correct: For V6, cannot_determine: Pearson correlation is 0.76 across 25 held-out recipes at fixed 1.2B size. This measures recipe-level association without varying scale or conditioning on pretraining loss.
source_check.locator_found: Page 8, paragraph reporting 25 held-out configurations; Figure 3(g).
source_check.problem: Imperfect fixed-size recipe association does not establish a partial scale-to-performance or pretraining-loss-to-performance relationship.

rows.subject: LayerMix runs in the higher-overtraining experiment (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Applied InfoLaw parameters fitted on the m = 3.6 data to predict results at a higher overtraining degree.
rows.measure: Agreement of higher-overtraining results with predicted information-loss scaling curve
rows.baseline: InfoLaw parameters fitted on the m = 3.6 data
rows.value: The new experimental points align with a new scaling-law curve; the m and m′ curves appear nearly parallel, with overtraining degree primarily shifting the intercept.
rows.note: No numerical prediction error is stated for this experiment.
rows.check: This tests transfer across overtraining regimes and an apparent intercept shift. The text and caption describe prediction using previously fitted parameters, but do not explain quantitatively how the new intercept is determined or report prediction errors. It does not independently establish orders-of-magnitude scale extrapolation or an ordinary compute power law.

rows.subject: RefinedWeb LayerMix runs (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Fit on HQ and LQ configurations and predicted loss for held-out MLQ configurations using RefinedWeb.
rows.measure: Absolute percentage error in predicted validation loss
rows.baseline: InfoLaw fitted on HQ and LQ configurations
rows.value: Maximum absolute error of 0.36% and mean absolute percentage error of 0.24%.
rows.note: For this verification set, the authors did not fit a λ(N) curve; they searched λ values for the three stated model sizes.
rows.check: This is held-out-recipe prediction at the same three model sizes used for fitting, not larger-scale extrapolation. Parameters are refitted on RefinedWeb and lambda is searched separately at each size; this is not transfer of the original fitted law to a new corpus.

source_check.locator_found: Appendix K, experimental setup, fitting and results; Figure 12.

rows.subject: LayerMix runs used to compare information-decay normalizations (aggregate)
rows.size_stated: 252M–7B in reported fit and extrapolation range
rows.operation_detail: Compared constant normalization with logarithmic normalization for the repetition-decay term.
rows.measure: Information accumulation and resulting loss prediction
rows.value: Constant normalization systematically overestimates accumulated information for large models trained with larger token budgets, producing overly optimistic loss predictions.
rows.note: The paper reports the comparison qualitatively and omits the plots.
rows.check: Change partial to observed: the reported failure of constant normalization supports dependence on functional-form choice. Evidence is qualitative, with plots and numerical comparison statistics omitted.

rows.subject: LayerMix runs used to compare information-decay normalizations (aggregate)
rows.size_stated: 252M–7B in reported fit and extrapolation range
rows.operation_detail: Compared power-law normalization with logarithmic normalization for the repetition-decay term.
rows.measure: Fit between information quantity and validation loss
rows.value: Power-law normalization failed to fit the information-validation-loss relationship; points remained scattered without the required power-law correlation.
rows.note: The paper reports the comparison qualitatively and omits the plots.
rows.check: Change absent to observed relative to V7: failure of the alternative normalization is evidence that fitting choices matter. The absent power-law correlation concerns the alternative information construction, not ordinary loss-versus-compute scaling.

rows.subject: Observed λ(N) values from LayerMix runs (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared logarithmic, exponential and power-law functional forms for λ as a function of non-embedding FLOPs/token N.
rows.measure: Fit and extrapolation of the λ–N relationship
rows.value: The logarithmic model achieved the best fit and extrapolation behavior.
rows.note: No numerical fit-comparison statistics are stated.
rows.check: This compares fits to an auxiliary parameter, lambda, rather than loss scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocation. It is a method-selection result and does not independently test V7.
